Culture · Film · Studio Ghibli

Spirited Away is 25. It is still finding new audiences.

Its final U.S. anniversary screening is tonight. A quarter-century after Chihiro entered the tunnel, the film’s survival story feels less like nostalgia than preparation for adulthood.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 21, 2026 at 08:10 JST · 6 min read

Twenty-five years after its Japanese release, Spirited Away is ending another journey tonight. GKIDS’ Studio Ghibli Fest lists October 21 as the final U.S. screening of the film’s five-day anniversary run, with the English-dubbed version scheduled after Japanese-language showings earlier in the week. The event also closes the distributor’s 2026 Ghibli festival.

A theatrical rerelease can look like the safest kind of programming: audiences already know the title, parents introduce it to children, and cinemas gain an event that streaming cannot duplicate. Yet the endurance of Hayao Miyazaki’s 125-minute film is not explained by familiarity alone. It continues to recruit viewers who were not born in 2001.

A child is not asked to conquer the world

Chihiro begins the film unhappy about moving home. Then her parents are transformed and she is forced to work in a bathhouse for spirits. The plot has witches, dragons and magic, but Miyazaki’s official director’s statement resists the structure of a simple battle between good and evil. Chihiro survives through attention, friendship, work and judgment.

That distinction is the film’s quiet engine. She does not discover that she is a chosen warrior. She learns how to act when adults are unreliable, rules are strange and every offer has a price. The fantasy gives a child’s anxiety physical form without reducing it to a villain who can be defeated.

The film grows with its audience because its victory is not domination. It is the ability to enter a confusing system without letting that system decide who you are.

Names, work and appetite

The bathhouse turns identity into administration. Yubaba takes part of Chihiro’s name and calls her Sen. Work gives the girl protection but also threatens to absorb her. Food becomes pleasure, greed and transformation. The train glides through a flooded landscape where the usual boundaries between towns, water and memory have dissolved.

These images are deeply connected to Japanese language and custom, yet they do not require a viewer to arrive with a glossary. A child understands the danger of forgetting a name. An adult understands the fear of signing a contract under pressure. The film is specific enough to feel made rather than manufactured, and open enough for different cultures to enter.

Why a cinema still matters

GKIDS presents Studio Ghibli Fest as a year-long return of the studio’s catalogue to U.S. theaters, with both Japanese-language and English-dubbed versions. The format is important. Streaming makes a film available; a scheduled screening makes it an appointment. It concentrates attention and creates a temporary public around work that might otherwise become background comfort viewing.

Associated Press reporting on the festival describes expanding theatrical demand even when the films are accessible at home. That is not necessarily a rejection of streaming. The two modes serve different desires: one provides access, the other provides occasion. Anniversary programming adds a reason to look again, while dual-language screenings let viewers choose between the performance they remember and the sound of the original production.

A Japanese classic that keeps moving

Spirited Away became an international reference point for Japanese animation, but “classic” can be a dangerous word. It can freeze a living film into an object people agree to admire. The theater run does the opposite. New viewers laugh at the soot sprites, fear No-Face, and sit through the long quiet of the train sequence in real time with strangers.

For Japan, that continuing appetite is cultural influence with unusual depth. The film does not sell a frictionless postcard. Its Japan is crowded with work, consumption, polluted rivers, courtesy, obligation and spirits that do not fit cleanly into moral categories. Audiences return not because the world is easy, but because it rewards another look.

Tonight’s screening is only “final” in the language of a festival schedule. The film has already outlived formats, distribution windows and generations of children. Chihiro walks back through the tunnel. The audience keeps entering.
